content: Dr. Ruby Dhalla, born on February 18, 1974, is a Canadian politician who has represented the Brampton—Springdale riding in the Canadian House of Commons since 2004 as a member of the Liberal Party of Canada. She, along with Nina Grewal of the British Columbia Conservative Party, became one of the first Sikh women to serve in the Canadian House of Commons. Dr. Dhalla was born in Winnipeg, Manitoba, to a family of immigrants from Punjab, India. At the age of ten, she gained international attention when she wrote a letter to then-Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, urging a peaceful resolution to the military actions at Punjab's Golden Temple. Gandhi personally responded to her letter and referenced it in a press conference shortly before her assassination. Dr. Dhalla earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Biochemistry with a minor in Political Science from the University of Winnipeg in 1995. She later moved to Toronto and graduated as a Doctor of Chiropractic from the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College in 1999. She co-owned a chain of chiropractic clinics in Toronto, Brampton, Mississauga, and Aurora, Ontario, with her brother, Neil Dhalla. In addition to her medical career, Dr. Dhalla pursued acting, spending six months in India and starring in a Bollywood-inspired Hindi-language film, Kyon? Kis Liye? (translated as Why? and for Whom?), which was filmed in Hamilton, Ontario. She also participated in the Miss India Canada pageant in 1993, where she placed second. Dr. Dhalla's political career began with her involvement in the Winnipeg Young Liberals and her support for Paul Martin's leadership bid in 2003. She was elected as the Liberal candidate for Brampton—Springdale in 2004, despite opposition from the local Liberal Party riding executive. She won the election and was appointed to the Standing Committee on Health. During her tenure, she organized significant relief efforts, including the Canada for Asia benefit concert for tsunami victims in 2005 and aid for earthquake victims in Pakistan later that year. She also advocated for accelerated foreign credential recognition for immigrants and supported same-sex marriage legislation in 2005. In the 2006 federal election, Dr. Dhalla was re-elected and became the Liberal Health Critic in the Official Opposition. She criticized the Conservative government on various issues, including conflicts of interest, the Prime Minister's absence from an international AIDS conference, and changes to immigration laws. She also supported Michael Ignatieff's leadership campaign and was later reassigned to the Social Development portfolio, where she opposed the privatization of childcare services and advocated for global tuberculosis eradication. In 2008, Dr. Dhalla introduced a Private Member's Bill calling for an apology for the 1914 Komagata Maru incident, which was unanimously passed. She faced a challenging re-election that year but ultimately defeated her Conservative opponent, Parm Gill, by a narrow margin. During this time, she also traveled to Punjab, India, where she advocated for stricter laws to protect married women from abuse. In 2009, Dr. Dhalla faced allegations of mistreatment of two Filipina caregivers hired to care for her mother. The caregivers accused her of seizing their passports and forcing them to perform tasks outside their job descriptions. Dr. Dhalla denied the allegations, stating she had no involvement in their hiring or supervision. Her brother, Neil Dhalla, also denied the claims, attributing the situation to an unscrupulous agency. A third caregiver later came forward with similar accusations. Dr. Dhalla stepped down as the Liberal Youth and Multiculturalism Critic and called for a federal ethics investigation to clear her name. The controversy was widely covered in the media, with some viewing it as a partisan attack. Despite the challenges, Dr. Dhalla has maintained her commitment to public service and advocacy for equality, immigrant rights, and social justice.
